content: Ceftriaxone should not be administered to patients who have a known allergy to cephalosporin antibiotics, as this could result in severe hypersensitivity reactions. Ceftriaxone is contraindicated in neonates who are 28 days old or younger, particularly in those with hyperbilirubinemia or those born prematurely. This is because in vitro studies have demonstrated that ceftriaxone can displace bilirubin from its binding to serum albumin, which may increase the risk of bilirubin encephalopathy in these vulnerable patients. Neonates who require, or are anticipated to require, treatment with calcium-containing intravenous solutions, such as continuous calcium-containing infusions used in parenteral nutrition, must not receive ceftriaxone. This is due to the risk of precipitation of ceftriaxone-calcium complexes, which can have serious clinical consequences. There have been reports of fatal outcomes in neonates who received ceftriaxone in conjunction with calcium-containing fluids. In some of these cases, crystalline material was found in the lungs and kidneys during autopsy. In certain instances, the same intravenous infusion line was used for both ceftriaxone and calcium-containing fluids, and precipitates were observed in the infusion line. At least one fatal case has been reported in a neonate where ceftriaxone and calcium-containing fluids were administered at separate times through different intravenous lines. In this case, no crystalline material was identified during autopsy. It is important to note that such adverse events have only been reported in neonates and not in older pediatric or adult patients.
